record.title: A preprint reports that finite precision breaks exact trajectory matching in Orthrus speculative decoding
record.summary: The v2 preprint compares Orthrus with its Qwen3-1.7B autoregressive reference across 1,190 prompts in 12 domains. Under BF16, exact token trajectories match in 45% of the released-checkpoint runs and 43% of an independently trained implementation; under FP16 the rate is 87%, and under FP32 it is 100% for the tested prompts. The authors report no systematic downstream-task degradation from divergence in their limited benchmarks. These are paper-reported results from two implementations at one model scale, not an independent reproduction.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across 1,190 prompts in 12 domains, the authors report exact trajectory matches for 45% of the released Orthrus checkpoint's BF16 generations and 43% of an independently trained Orthrus implementation; FP16 matching is 87%, and FP32 matching is 100% on this prompt set.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that trajectory divergence does not correspond to systematic degradation on their evaluated downstream benchmarks; point estimates vary with inference precision and are not established as statistically significant improvements or declines.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The v2 preprint specifies exact token-sequence matching as its operational test of losslessness and documents the two Qwen3-1.7B-based implementations, inference precisions and 12-domain prompt set used in its reported comparison.

contradictory_evidence: The paper reports no systematic downstream-task degradation despite frequent BF16 trajectory divergence; exact sequence inequality does not by itself establish lower task quality.
FP32 exactly matched all 1,190 prompts in the reported test, showing the observed divergence depends on numerical precision and tested configuration.

evidence_gaps.description: The linked implementation and reported comparison were not run in this review, and independent replication was not inspected.
The paper studies Qwen3-1.7B-based Orthrus implementations and does not establish transfer to other scales or speculative-decoding architectures.
The study does not measure effects of trajectory divergence on long reasoning traces or tool-calling behavior.

brief.importance_rationale: If practical low-precision inference changes exact output trajectories in methods described as lossless, this can affect reproducibility claims and how inference-acceleration systems are evaluated. Consequence is meaningful for systems relying on exact trajectory preservation; the paper does not show systematic task degradation and tests one Qwen3-1.7B-based architecture.
limitations: Author-reported preprint results; this review did not execute code/checkpoints or independently reproduce the measurements.

The experiments cover two Qwen3-1.7B-based Orthrus implementations, greedy decoding, one hardware/software setup and a curated 1,190-prompt set; behavior at other scales and in other acceleration architectures is unknown.
The authors do not identify which computational stage causes the precision-dependent divergence.
Downstream evaluation covers GSM8K, HumanEval and IFEval and does not test chain-of-thought propagation or tool selection; trajectory divergence does not establish practical task harm.
Exact token trajectory matching is the paper's chosen operational criterion for losslessness; other definitions, including distributional equivalence, are distinct.
brief.summary: The v2 preprint compares Orthrus with its Qwen3-1.7B autoregressive reference across 1,190 prompts in 12 domains. Under BF16, exact token trajectories match in 45% of the released-checkpoint runs and 43% of an independently trained implementation; under FP16 the rate is 87%, and under FP32 it is 100% for the tested prompts. The authors report no systematic downstream-task degradation from divergence in their limited benchmarks. These are paper-reported results from two implementations at one model scale, not an independent reproduction.

technical.claimed_result: For greedy decoding on the reported prompts, exact Orthrus/reference token-sequence matching was 45% for the released checkpoint and 43% for the independent implementation under BF16, 87% for both under FP16, and 100% for both under FP32.
technical.demonstrated_result: The authors document a direct token-trajectory comparison over 1,190 prompts in 12 domains and report precision-specific outcomes; this review did not execute the implementation or reproduce them.
technical.mechanism: Compare every generated token index from Orthrus against its frozen autoregressive Qwen3 reference until end-of-sequence or the generation limit; any difference marks the sequence as divergent.
technical.regime: Two Qwen3-1.7B-based Orthrus implementations; greedy generation, up to 128 new tokens, 1,190 prompts across 12 domains, eager attention on an RTX 3090; BF16, FP16 and FP32 inference.
technical.reproducibility: The preprint reports its experimental setup and links author implementation materials; neither code nor checkpoints were executed in this review.
technical.strongest_baseline: The corresponding frozen autoregressive Qwen3-1.7B model under matched prompts and inference precision; FP32 served as a higher-precision comparison and yielded exact matches on all tested prompts.

brief.title: A preprint reports that finite precision breaks exact trajectory matching in Orthrus speculative decoding
brief.why_it_matters: The study makes the operational meaning of lossless inference concrete: exact output-sequence equivalence can fail under practical low-precision inference even when the decoding algorithm is intended to preserve its reference trajectory. If confirmed across systems, evaluations of accelerated decoding should report precision and exact-match criteria alongside task scores. The results do not show systematic task degradation or establish how often divergence changes consequential reasoning or tool use.
